opus-5.5.text:
I think it's mostly because Tsinghua is where I really grew up, intellectually and as a person. I came in quite young, and those years are when you figure out what you actually care about. A lot of who I am today, how I think about problems and what I consider good taste in research, was shaped there.

Part of it is the people. You're surrounded by classmates who are incredibly smart and driven, and that pushes you without anyone saying a word. You see someone working on something hard at two in the morning, and you think, okay, I should take this more seriously. Many of those friendships are still the most important ones in my life, and many of those people are now doing remarkable things all over the world.

Part of it is the teachers. Some of them gave me a lot of freedom and trust when I hadn't really proven anything yet. They let me try ambitious things and fail, and they took my ideas seriously. That kind of support matters enormously at that age, and I don't think I fully appreciated it until later.

And there's something about the place itself: the campus, the history, the feeling that you're part of a long line of people who wanted to do something meaningful. When I go back now, walking past the old buildings, the lake, the places where we used to argue about physics or the future, there's a strong sense of home.

So it's not really about the institution as a brand. It's that so many formative moments happened there, and I feel I owe it a lot. If I can, I'd like to give some of that back someday.

r001.rationale: The response credits Tsinghua with shaping him and with teachers giving him freedom and trust, but it does not say his affection comes from the school’s willingness to give people equal opportunities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because Tsinghua gave me the four most formative years of my life, and gave them to me at exactly the moment when I had no idea who I was yet.

I went in as a kid from a small place who was good at taking exams. That's basically all I knew about myself. And the first thing Tsinghua did was put me in a room with people who were far more talented than I was, which was humbling in a very useful way. In Yao Class in particular, you very quickly stop thinking of yourself as "the smart one" and start thinking about what you actually want to do with your mind. That shift is the most important thing that happened to me there.

The second thing is freedom. People sometimes imagine Tsinghua as this very structured, very engineering-minded place, and it is, but at the same time there was an enormous amount of room to wander. I spent a lot of time in the library reading things that had nothing to do with my courses. I took classes in philosophy, in history, I argued with friends late into the night about questions we had no business thinking we could answer. Nobody told me that was a waste of time. Looking back, a lot of the way I think about intelligence and agents today comes from those detours rather than from the formal curriculum.

And then there are the people. The friends I made there are still the people I call when I'm stuck on something, not just technically but in life. Some of my teachers, like Yao Qizhi and others, modeled a kind of seriousness and gentleness at the same time that I'm still trying to live up to. When you're nineteen and you see someone who has achieved everything and still treats a student's half-formed question with real curiosity, that leaves a mark.

So the affection isn't really about the campus or the name. It's gratitude. Tsinghua took a very unfinished person and gave him the space, the pressure, and the company to start becoming someone. You don't forget the place that did that for you.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes his affection to formative experiences, intellectual freedom, relationships, and gratitude. It does not say Tsinghua gave people equal opportunities.

astra-6.text: I think it’s really an affection for the people and for that period of my life. When I think of Tsinghua, I think of the teachers, classmates, and friends who helped shape how I approach problems. Being around people who are curious and ambitious encourages you to ask more of yourself. What stays with me is that sense of growing together. So the attachment is personal—it’s gratitude for the people and experiences that helped make me who I am.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his affection to people, relationships, and formative experiences, but does not mention Tsinghua giving people equal opportunities.

sol-6.1.text: I think a lot of that affection comes from the people and the sense of possibility. When you’re surrounded by people who are curious and ambitious, you start asking bigger questions yourself. And later, what stays with you isn’t just what you learned in class—it’s the friendships, the conversations, and the way that environment helped you grow. For me, that’s what makes Tsinghua feel special.

r001.rationale: The response credits affection to the people, friendships, conversations, and a sense of possibility, but does not say Tsinghua gives people equal opportunities.
